After building 20+ custom reporting dashboards and advising 35+ web3 companies on analytics, these are the 3 reasons I've found on why tracking in web3 growth is so difficult. 

1/ NO ONE SIZE FITS ALL 
In Web2, there are staple measurement and tracking tools: 

Web: Google Analytics, Matamo, Posthog
MMPs: Branch, Appsflyer 
Product: Amplitude 
Ecom Attribution: Hyros, Triple Whale 

Then there are tools like Segment, Tableau, Domo to combine all sources and visualize together. 

In Web3, we have 100+ wallets, 20+ chains with over $100m TVL, and numerous product categories that require different measurement models.

Product categories here can include:
Exchanges - cex/dex
Defi protocol 
Ecom with hardware wallets 
Marketplaces 
Ecosystems 
Events 
Social 
Gaming
Basically web3 is the "new internet" right? So every product category in web2 can exist here as well. 

Just like Web2, each of these product categories come with all these other variables like web page, web app, mobile app. 

Now combine that with all the wallets, chains, multiple contracts, web2 native data, and you can see how resource-intensive and custom a winning solution for a web3 company can be. 

2/ TOOLING CAN'T KEEP UP 

Every new chain requires tools to adapt. EVM is easiest, but imagine Cosmos and dapp chains. Or when a new chain pops up. Theres 100 chains out there with $2.5M tvl. 

Then, some protocols like staking pools or dexs have multiple smart contracts, on multiple chains, each requiring custom-builds from tools to adapt to. The easiest project to track is a single smart contract evm, with a wallet connect. But this is not always the case. 

This is expensive and developer-intensive. Especially in a time where funding might be running slim on both the brand side, and tooling set side, and an audience crunch in the market. 

3/ NATURE OF BLOCKCHAIN & PRICE SPECULATION

Everything lives on the blockchain, forever, but consider Inflows /outflows come from CEXs, bridges, p2p which means you lose can lose the flow of funds at some point. You also can lose entry/outflow points on the web2 side. Say someone clicks through a newsletter to to a crypto casino. You can combine that user's web2 data an click to the signup on the casino. But then they fund the wallet with Binance, and they outflow back to Binance. You have no way to track what this customer has done onchain before or after. So you're back to building an audience segment based off the web2 data points. 

On top of that, even if you do use wallet analytics to segment users, I believe the main narrative of the space is purely speculative. Most of the volume and holdings in one's wallet is based off price goes up, not interest (e.g. If i buy a game NFT I might be buying it because I think it will appreciate in value, not because I'm a gamer)

This combined with a small audience (600k active wallet addresses on L2s and ETH according to Dune, + consider 1 unique user may have multiple addresses) sets us up for dismal data sizes to make coherent judgments

HOW TO MANAGE? 
- Don't dismiss web2 data. Email, socials, engagement, entry points. 
- Map out your flow first, find measurement and tracking tools that can capture the priority parts of this journey 
- Use blended metrics if needed, we use this all the time in web2, especially with GDPR and Apple's notorius iOS 14 change in privacy and online ads 
- Personalize and customize. The 20+ dashboards we built for clients were each different. To measure successfully and effectively for growth, you need to tailor it to your flow

CLIPPING: crypto marketers are just discovering what it is. Here's a breakdown and how it's used for growth

The purpose of clipping is to get your video content distributed at scale. 
1. You attract editors and creators via your own pages (like the crypto marketers we're seeing now) or use existing networks or platforms like Whop
2. Drop a brief and video/folder of content to editors and creators
3. They find the best parts of the video and make short form clips 
4. They upload that to different sites like Tiktok, X, Youtube, etc

You then pay based on how much reach and virality the video gets.

- Typical payouts are $2-5 CPM with some caps. This mean you pay $2-5 per every 1000 views
- Although, I do see a Polymarket campaign live right now paying $0.20 CPM lol
- Guidelines are important to set: logo visibility, caption/hashtags, how long the post should be live for, engagement % requirement, and most importantly: geos that your page targets (most split this into tiers) 
- It's a brute force action. Clippers who are successful have a sense of what could go viral from the hook, the editing, the content and then product at high-frequency 
- It's similar to our tactics for Tiktok and IG Reel growth. Post 1-3 times a day from a group of accounts and adjust hooks until you find things that work

Just finished a hiring round for our growth team. A ton of dms and resumes flooded in from this post

I know there’s a lot of people looking for their next career chapter. I was reflecting on what I signals I use to filter applications and invite to first round interviews: 

Bucket A: Specialist in a specific channel that is hands on (e.g. performance marketing, lifecycle marketing) 
- Firstly requires a clear view of OKRs and how to achieve them to know what roles to build around  
- Some knowledge in how time intensive each speciality is and if it requires dedicated talent doing it full time, or a generalist type (this is changing with AI) 
- Should be visible in a candidates resume with quantifiable results 
- As a candidate, you should also reflect knowledge of the skill with the exact tool stacks you’ve used in your cv 

Bucket B: Generalist with domain expertise 
- For example, a marketing lead or growth marketer who wore multiple hats but worked at a competitor, breakout app, or company in similar category 
- Requires awareness of and identifying breakout companies, competitors, similar cos in your category (some carry more weight) 
- Ideally comes with some edge based on that exact vertical (existing relationships, knowledge in best converting channels, angles, geos etc) 
- When applying as a candidate, highlight companies you’ve worked at that are most similar to the job with call outs on how you helped them grow 

Other signals I look for: 
- Ability to position themselves concisely in cold dms 
- How metrics and responsibilities are framed in cv
- Existing owned distribution: do they have any social channels or media they’ve built up themselves 
- Proactivity and grit signaled by any entrepreneurial experience 
- AI-native (usually more deeply sourced in interview) 

Reference checks are also important in key hiring decisions, if you’re an applicant, expect this to happen

After hiring 15+ people since the start of this year and conducting 80+ interviews, I'm reflecting on our T-Shaped Web3 Marketer framework. 

1. Just having agency or brand experience in tech, consumer, product is not enough.  The people that thrive at Hype live onchain. They are immersed into crypto culture. They mint, trade, stake, farm, claim. They spend time on crypto Twitter, Hey, Warpcast. They're in 237482 telegram groups and discords. They also understand the nuances of crypto culture which brings me to...

2. The "Web3 Knowledge" piece is getting more segmented as the space matures. Specifically at Hype, most of our work is in bringing DeFi protocols, ecosystems, and dev infra to market. The type of knowledge for growth in these segments tends to be a bit more technical. Consumer crypto, meme coins, and say, a modular restaking protocol all attract different types of users with their own culture-bubbles online. 

3. I would add in innovation and adaptability to our framework. Someone who is living and breathing onchain culture will see how often the metas change. 
Year 1 for me at Hype was a lot of L1 ecosystems, nfts, games. It birthed our DevRel teams as we quickly learned we needed to know how to connect with builders. We did a lot of whitelisting campaigns. 
Year 2 was dev infra, we did a lot of launches in a bear market which was less noisy 
Today and in Q1 2024, there are many launches and TGEs. 

The space's metas change - LSTs/LRTs are hot, DePin, memecoins are in now

Marketing metas in web3 also change (and change fast) - airdrop farming was big.. watch it move towards retrospective airdrops and other reward mechanisms after users get desensitized. Brand marketing will continue to crush this year as projects try to stand out in all the noise. 

All this to say, it's exciting to see the space continuing to mature to a point where "web3 marketer" is a vague term. We are still very early and far from PMF (unless you're a stablecoin, exchange, wallet) which means the audience targeted is a niche and requires deep understanding. IF you are someone that lives and breathes onchain, please dm me as we are always looking for the best to join our team.
